newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: POLL-Ayala Land H1 seen flat, best to wait.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Ayala Land H1 seen flat, best to wait.

text.p: Its first half performance will be uninspiring but if a property company was to be picked investors would choose Ayala Land Inc, analysts said on Tuesday.

A Reuters poll of seven stock brokerages showed that Ayala Land, the country's biggest property company, would post a 2.75 percent drop in its first six months net profit to 2.47 billion pesos ($94 million), down from the year-ago 2.54 billion.
But full year 1997 could see the company recovering and net profit could rise 18 percent to reach 4.89 billion pesos, average numbers from the poll showed.
For a company that converted what was wilderness just 40 years ago into an area called Makati, the country's premier business district, the past six months have been rather dull.

"Their first half will be flattish. It might be even less than that unless they do something unique like selling shares of a subsidiary or a plot of land," said one analyst who did not want to be named for fear of annoying one of the most prestigious companies in the country.

Ayala Land is part of Ayala Corp, the Philippines' oldest conglomerate, that traces its roots to 1834. Since then the Ayala family has remained in firm control of the company and Jaime Zobel de Ayala of the seventh generation is now chairman.
Their name is so prominent that Makati's main street is called Ayala Avenue. This used to be the runway of a private Ayala airport and the control tower still stands there.
But in the company's first half performance, there was no evidence of its high-flying credentials, analysts said.
"In the second quarter, there was a slowdown in take-up. Demand was affected by all the negative publicity of a property glut," said Noel Reyes, research head, Anscor Hagedorn Securities.
In May, Manila's property stocks were battered after the market was gripped by rumours of an impending crash.
"I believe it is mostly perception. Once people realise their fears are unfounded, they will start buying," Reyes said.
Reyes said prospects for lower interest rates in the second half of the year would also boost property demand.
Last month, the Philippine Central Bank raised its overnight lending rate to 20 percent from 13 to protect the peso from speculation as a result of the financial crisis in Thailand.
At present, it is at 15 percent but the Central Bank would like to lower it as soon as the Thai situation permits.
Bernadette Tamayo, analyst at BPI Capital Corp, said Ayala Land was a favourite because it had a wide range of products.
The over-supply in the property market was said to have been restricted to expensive office and residential premises and Ayala Land did not depend on that alone, she said.
Ayala Land is now developing an industrial park and company officials said its new investments would be in middle-income housing and infrastucture and on developments outside Manila.
The rural market for property was seen as the brightest spots for the sector. "Provincial property plays - Screamingly cheap," brokerage Asia Equity said in its June report.
One of them, Cebu Holdings Inc's operations were geared towards the fast-growing and dynamic Visayas and Mindanao areas," it said. Cebu Holdings is 47 percent owned by Ayala Land.
